questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to practice my spanish and South America is a melting pot of new experiences, cultures, nature and lots of other aspects that made it a natural choice. Santiago has always been a relatively safe city in SA, which i can now confirm, it really is safe enough that it does not feel any different than capital cities in southern europe.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As a principle, I cannot rate it 10, as that means perfection and nothing ever is. With that being said, Chile and Santiago in itself were amazing and offered so much culturally, academically and socially.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: There is a great office at the Universidad de Chile, PME, which handle all the exchange students. There were two zoom meetings before arrival with general information and I also had contact with them through email as i needed some course descriptions.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Universidad de Chile was extremely helpful with all the information I needed - that does not mean that they solved the problems though. One thing to remember is that you have arrived in South America and therefore deadlines is now something negotiable. The class sign up was only done two weeks into the semester and the first day of school, I therefore didn't have the formal sign-up. But as the office said - there is no problem, 99% of the exchange students get the classes that they want (and I also did) it is just because their systems take time and the administration is on vacation.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Every faculty has a PME assistant - it goes way faster if you contact the PME assistant at your faculty than the general PME administration and often, they will also give you better, more detailed, answers.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found it before i left Copenhagen and in hindsight, I should've relaxed with the danish attitude of needing to have everything in order before departure. Almost every other exchange student from other nationalities just arrived in Santiago and stayed at hostels until they found housing, soemthing which works extremely well in Santiago. Seriously, every single one of my friends found housing within 2-3 weeks, there is no need to do it from home and just ending up paying a higher price!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There is no on-campus housing, so everybody will be living off campus. You will probably read Santiago guides before departure to determine in which area to live and when i did, every guide talked about Las Condes and Vitacura - DO NOT LIVE THERE. It is the same as living in Hellerup (rich/fancy area where it is only residential). There are plenty of cool, SAFE neighbourhoods in Santiago. I lived in Providencia, next to Baquedano station and that was amazing. I can recommend Lastarria, Providencia, Barrio Italia and Barrio Yungay (a little bit more rough in the edges, but okay nonetheless).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
There are three kinds of housing:
1) The fancy student housing (LivinXX) which is a whole building only with students in nice 2-4 people apartments with a pool, study room, gym and a 24h reception with guard. This is also the most expensive option. I know people who lived here and it is indeed much nicer inside, think european standard living, yet for the price, i cannot justify it - best option is to make friends with someone who lives there so you're invited to the parties!
2) Option two is the medium price range and what i did - I lived with Santiago Exchange, a company specialised in student housing and with houses around Santiago. It was cheaper than Livinxx but also didn't have any of the extra amenities. It was fun, we were 30 students in a big house, very hostel vibes.
3) Option three is the cheapest option and also the option i would recommend, i wished i had done this myself. Through the website
compartodepto.cl
(like boligportalen in cph) you will find lots of houses that are rented out for students, they are 100% the cheapest option, you will get a good mix of international students and chilean students and mostly, you will end up in houses where the rules are a lot less strict than in the more formal arrangements in option 1 and 2. You need to be able to keep your cool though, you will normally contact the owner on compartodepto and then go see the house a couple days later and then sign the contract and move in a couple days after, so you normally need to wait until you have arrived. It is worth the wait though and I regret not having waited.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As said, it was easy and I did get all the courses I wanted, but it will be a long process and you cannot get any formal paper saying you are signed up before after semester start.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You send in a wish list of courses before semester start. When school then starts, the first two weeks are for trying out and seeing how you like the classes. Important info here is that there are no "forelæsninger" everything is class teaching. Depending on popularity of the class, each subject is split into 2-4 classes. That means that if you have a class like "Politica Latinoamerica" you will have Politica Latinoamerica.1, Politica Latinoamerica.2, Politica Latinoamerica.3 and Politica Latinoamerica.4. 
This means that every number has a different schedule and a different teacher. This is extremely good for us exchange students because this means we can take the class that fits the best into our schedule AND most importantly, try out the different teachers. For me, the most crucial was understanding the professor and i therefore went to the different classes and saw which teachers mumbled, who spoke super fast etc. so I could limit my spanish language issue the most possible. Therefore the two weeks were actually a really good idea from Universidad de Chile and super helpful. 

After the two weeks, you send in your final wishlist with the designated 'number' of your class and you're placed and become an offical part of the class.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The PME assistant at Facultad de Gobierno was extremely helpful and I just went to campus and walked up to her office anytime I had questions, no reservation needed.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all of the classes i wanted and also the desired 'number' for each class. 99% of all exchange students get this, so please, do not worry.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be open to their systems and try out the different teachers for each class, i promise you dont have to stay with the 60yo mumbling man.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have a lot of really cool subjects and you are able to take all levels of classes and also on two different faculties, so it is only the requirements of KU that limit us.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I had classes with both first year students, third year students and electives with people of all ages. You are free to do whatever you want.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There is no "forelæsninger" only class teaching, which is different, but not necessarily bad. I felt the difficulty level was low compared to UCPH, because it is way more memorizing and being able to say a bit about the readings. They also don't have one final exam at the end but rather 3-4 tests throughout the semester and therefore, in a test situation, you have less material to focus on and it is fresh in your mind.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Fenómenos Macroeconómicos AP01306-1
Política Comparada I CP1203-2
Política Latinoamericana CP3202-1
Desafíos de la Diversidad Culturel desde Latinoamerica ELEGOB06-1

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really liked having an elective course as it was with an "outside professor" who only came in because this was her field of study. The people enrolled in this class were also all super motivated because they had chosen it, not because they needed it. It was very fun. I also loved the course "Política Latinoamericana" which was super interesting.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Chile is by no means super cheap and it did suprise me that i felt like Madrid/Rome prices in that it was cheaper than Copenhagen, but also not dirt cheap. I made sure to be out a lot and try lots of things, so I spent more money than I thought i would, but it was definetly worth it.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Almost all museums are free for students, so use them!!!
Restaurants were more expensive than i thought they would be, but a good empanada is only about 14 kroner, so eat those instead!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were a ton of options, both sports focused and academically. I didn't attend any of them though, they are almost all located out in Nuñoa at the Facultad de Filosofía y Humanidades (Juan Gomez). This takes 30 mins by bus from the city center and I had no other classes at the faculty, so honestly, I was just too lazy to go there. I have some friends who had their courses at that faculty though and they attended extracurriculars and loved it.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Lots of different sports, everything is shown in the course catalogue.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Lots of bars and clubs in Santiago make "theme nights" and i met a ton of people by going to these. They are a bit kitsch, admitted, but you meet people there and then when you hang out again, you just do it at a bar of your choosing, so no need to go more than a few times - it's just networking!

I also need to give a special shout out to MiercolesPO (find them on Instagram), which is an exchange student club - and yes, it is just as american frat-coded as you think, but literally every exchange student goes to these parties every wednesday and so you know everybody, the music is okay and it's a good way to meet up with people you dont see everyday at your faculties. Do it!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Chile is an enormous country and with so much to offer. I will try to list as many places as possible:
1) Cajon del Maipo. This is 30 mins outside of Santiago and was my first trip, it is easy to get to with public transport and a wonderful place for hiking and small villages with markets. Very easy weekend destination. 
2) La Serena + Valle del Elqui. My second destination, we rented a car and drove up there (btw renting a car is easy and with no fuss, big recommendation). Beautiful and with lots of history - try Pisco at one of the old distilleries!
3) Pichilemu. This is out on the coast and the unofficial surfing capital of the world apparently - there is a great vibe, other internationals and of course, the water is amazing (cold though!). 
4) Santa Cruz. The fancy wine area of Chile, we went here as a part of a larger roadtrip and it was beautiful, we might as well have driven around France - not necessarily the most chilean place, but beautiful nonetheless. 
5) Parque Nacional Altos del Lircay and the Laguna del Maule. This is probably one of the most beautiful places I have ever been and it is rarely mentioned in guide books so i 100% recommend going and reserving a little hut up in the mountain and do beautiful hiking and roadtrips!
6) Mendoza. A lot of students went here in the middle of the semester as a way of refreshing their tourist visa (the student visa is expensive and takes time and nobody checks if you have it - just stay on the tourist visa!). When you cross the border to Argentina you get 3 more months and it works perfectly and mendoza is a beautiful wine town, so win-win!
7) Valparaiso/Viña del Mar. For some reason every guide book talks about these destinations but wow, so overrated. Go visit of course if you want but there are a thousand places in Chile that are more worth your time!
8) Chiloe. The most beautiful island down in Northern Patagonia, it just has a special atmosphere. Go visit!
9) Torres del Paine. Not much to say, it should really be one of the worlds natural wonders - it is expensive, be warned, but 100% worth it. The amount of foreigners is scary though, definetly not a destination where you will find chileans, it is too expensive for them. 
10) The rest of the coast next to Santiago - I really liked Isla Negra and Algarrobo
11) The region Norte Grande. I did an amazing road trip up north in Chile by the cities Iquique and Arica and visited the Parinacotta volcano in 5000 meters altitude and it was amazing. There were almost no people, they are all down in San Pedro de Atacama, and it was cheap - huge recommendation. 
12) Rapa Nui. I ended my exchange with one week on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) and it was absolutely amazing, what an experience. 

Chile has a very extensive network of busses and my main form of transport was nightbuses or renting a car between friends. Go see all this amazing country has to offer!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I had visited South America before and I knew a little bit of what to expect - you are in the salsa dancing, reggaeton listening part of the world and you should act accordingly! As danes, we can be a bit 'boring' in comparison, so the goal is to find a golden middle, where you enjoy what Chile has to offer BUT where you're also careful that you don't lose yourself in the process and only live in the night.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I must be honest, I only had a couple chilean students. Chileans are super friendly and it will be easy to strike up a conversation with them. I had some issues with the obvious age difference - most of the students will be 19-21 years old and they will also be in another place mentally. That does not mean that everybody is horrible and my chilean friends showed me lots of cool corners of Santiago and gave me good tips, but it was definetly easier to connect with other internationals.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: No toilet paper in the toilet - seriously, even after 6 months, it is just such a habit that I had to remind myself every day.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I was able to get out of my bubble and really enjoy public dancing on the streets, karaoke, just generally taking up more space in the public sphere. As a dane, it is refreshing to see that it is possible to live differently.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Go to all the events (especially MiercolesPO!) and meet as many as possible. There are tons of different universities around Santiago and because i participated in these events, I knew people from different universities and different majors - a huge plus. 
2) Please wait with booking your accomodation, you will get rewarded and end up with the coolest place. 
3) Embrace the spanish! It is hard and they speak very fast, but with a little willpower, you will get far.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Take longs walks aroudn Santiago and get to know your new city, there are so many cultural institutions that are just waiting to be discovered!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting so many people from all over the world and finding out how much we actually have in common!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: All my courses were in Spanish and my level was definetly not high enough when i arrived. Do your best, talk to your teachers, they only want to help you. I ended up passing all my courses, so it is possible!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: ¡Viva Chile!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
